solution.concept_anchor: Token currency failure — private minting as the decisive mechanism
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'merchants refusing to accept the tokens from the outset' is deceptive because it contains a partial truth — merchants eventually refused — but the claim 'from the outset' is incorrect; initial acceptance was reported, with the breakdown coming later.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: factors that directly contributed to the actual historical failure of MBT's token currency experiment.
Option (a) — private minting of counterfeit tokens: directly caused the currency's devaluation and is a primary documented failure reason — belongs.

Option (b) — merchants refusing from the outset: initial acceptance was reported (even in temple offerings per Battuta); mass refusal came later, not from the outset — does not accurately describe the failure mechanism and contains a temporal error.
Option (c) — hoarding of silver tankas: a documented consequence of Gresham's Law operating during the experiment — belongs as a genuine failure reason.

Option (d) — Mongol invasion disrupting minting infrastructure: Mongol threats were the background fiscal pressure that motivated the experiment, not a factor that caused its failure; no Mongol invasion disrupted MBT's minting during this period — does not belong as a failure cause.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) carries a partial truth — merchants did eventually refuse — and the detail 'from the outset' is subtle enough that students may overlook it. The real odd one out is (d), which attributes the failure to Mongol disruption of minting infrastructure, which has no historical support. The Mongol threat was the context for the experiment's introduction, not the cause of its failure. Students who know Mongols were a background threat may accept (d) without scrutiny.
solution.final_explanation:
The token currency experiment failed through several interacting mechanisms, and distinguishing genuine failure factors from plausible-sounding fabrications tests precise knowledge.

• Option (a) — Belongs: Private minting of counterfeit tokens was the decisive failure mechanism. Without infrastructure to prevent it, anyone could produce base-metal tokens and pass them as legitimate currency — rapidly destroying the tokens' credibility.
• Option (b) — Does NOT belong (odd one out by partial truth): Merchants did eventually refuse the tokens, but 'from the outset' is historically inaccurate. Ibn Battuta records initial acceptance — even Hindus used the tokens in religious contexts. Refusal built gradually as the currency's credibility collapsed.
• Option (c) — Belongs: Silver tankas were hoarded rather than used, as per Gresham's Law ('bad money drives out good'). This removed the reliable monetary medium from circulation, worsening the crisis.
• Option (d) — Does NOT belong (the actual odd one out): Mongol invasion of MBT's minting infrastructure is not a documented historical event. Mongol pressure motivated the experiment's introduction but played no role in its failure mechanism.

Value Addition:
• Gresham's Law — 'bad money drives out good' — is the classical economic principle operating in this episode.
• The experiment required approximately the same institutional infrastructure as modern central banking — which took centuries to develop.
• MBT eventually had to redeem the tokens for silver at a significant loss to the treasury before withdrawing the scheme.

solution.concept_anchor: Vijayanagara and Bahmani founding — dates and contexts

statement_analysis.statement: The Vijayanagara kingdom was founded in 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, who had previously been officers under the Delhi Sultanate.
statement_analysis.reason: 1336 is the accepted founding date of Vijayanagara; Harihara and Bukka were indeed associated with the Delhi Sultanate before establishing their independent kingdom — both elements are accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: The Bahmani Sultanate was founded in 1347 by a noble known as Hasan Gangu, who assumed the title Bahman Shah after successfully rebelling against Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Deccan administration.
statement_analysis.reason: 1347, Hasan Gangu, the title Bahman Shah, and rebellion against MBT's Deccan administration are all accurately described — this is a fully correct statement.

statement_analysis.statement: The prolonged Doab famine (approximately 1335–1342) was entirely a product of MBT's policy failures and had no independent climatic or environmental dimension.
statement_analysis.reason: The Doab famine had both a policy dimension (excessive taxation) and an environmental dimension (drought/famine conditions); attributing it 'entirely' to policy failure and denying any climatic component is historically inaccurate — the compounding of natural disaster and bad policy was central to the episode.

statement_analysis.statement: Among the rebellions during MBT's reign, the revolt of Ain-ul-Mulk Multani is historically significant because he was a trusted noble of the Sultanate, making his defection a marker of systemic breakdown rather than merely regional discontent.
statement_analysis.reason: Ain-ul-Mulk Multani is specifically noted because his loyalty to MBT was previously established — a trusted noble's rebellion signals institutional failure at the highest level, not merely peripheral dissent.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is the strongest distractor because three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct, but students who accept Statement 3's 'entirely policy-driven' claim without scrutinising the word 'entirely' will mark all four as correct, leading to option (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 1336, Harihara + Bukka, Delhi Sultanate officers — all accurate; Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: 1347, Hasan Gangu, Bahman Shah, rebellion against MBT — all accurate; Statement 2 is correct.

Statement 3: 'entirely a product of MBT's policy failures' with 'no environmental dimension' — scope-extension making a partial truth false; drought/climatic factors are documented; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statement 4: Ain-ul-Mulk Multani as a trusted noble whose rebellion signals systemic breakdown — accurately described; Statement 4 is correct. Three correct (1, 2, 4) → answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap and scope-extension in Statement 3 are the traps here. Students who know the Doab famine occurred during MBT's reign and know it was exacerbated by taxation may accept 'entirely a product of policy failure' without noting that drought/climate conditions were independently operating. The word 'entirely' and the phrase 'no independent climatic dimension' make a true partial claim into a false absolute — a classic scope-extension mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
MBT's reign saw a convergence of policy failures and natural disasters, and the question tests whether students can distinguish between partial truths and fully accurate statements.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 1336, Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, former Delhi Sultanate officers — all elements are historically accurate for Vijayanagara's founding.
• Statement 2 — Correct: 1347, Hasan Gangu (Bahman Shah), rebellion against MBT's Deccan administration — all elements accurate for the Bahmani Sultanate's founding.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Doab famine had both dimensions — MBT's tax hike created fiscal stress, but underlying drought conditions made it catastrophic. Attributing it 'entirely' to policy and denying any climatic factor is a false absolute. The compounding of nature and policy is precisely the historical lesson.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Ain-ul-Mulk Multani's rebellion is historiographically significant because trusted loyalists rarely rebel — his defection signals that even the core of MBT's support structure had broken down, indicating systemic rather than merely regional crisis.

Value Addition:
• Vijayanagara (1336) and Bahmani (1347) — both founded during MBT's reign — permanently ended Delhi's effective sovereignty over South India.
• The Doab famine's environmental dimension aligns with recent historical research into climatic fluctuations in the 14th century affecting agricultural civilisations across Asia.
• Ain-ul-Mulk Multani's rebellion is documented in Barani's chronicle — his eventual fate after the rebellion is also recorded.

solution.concept_anchor: State agricultural credit — takkavi loan precedent and implementation failure
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students may identify the 'demonstration farm' element as the primary policy tool and select option (c), which focuses on extension services, without recognising that the primary state instrument described in the scenario is credit disbursement — matching takkavi loans.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): market price controls regulate the commodity market externally — the scenario describes direct credit disbursement to farmers, not price-fixing.

Confirm (b): state-sponsored agricultural loans (takkavi/Sondhar loans) are the instrument that matches the scenario — direct credit to farmers to restore cultivation, with accompanying risk of fund embezzlement by intermediary officials.

Eliminate (c): agricultural extension services (knowledge/technique transfer) are partially reflected in the Diwan-i-Kohi's demonstration farms, but the primary policy tool in the scenario is credit, not extension services alone.
Eliminate (d): granary-based food security (grain reserves for price stabilisation) was Alauddin Khalji's instrument — not the primary response to agrarian collapse through credit disbursement.
solution.final_explanation:
A government facing severe agrarian distress following excessive taxation and famine conditions designs a scheme to restore agricultural productivity. The state allocates funds disbursed as loans to farmers, creating new government offices to manage disbursement. Field officials are entrusted with distributing credit and supervising cultivation on state-owned land. Three years later, an audit reveals that officials have falsified crop records, funds have been misappropriated, and cultivated area has barely increased despite the large investment.

The applicable policy instrument is state-sponsored agricultural credit (takkavi/Sondhar loans, supplemented by Diwan-i-Kohi demonstration farms). This matches precisely MBT's response to the Doab agrarian collapse.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Market price controls regulate exchange without addressing agricultural productivity or financing cultivation — a different instrument for a different problem.
• Option (b) — Correct: State agricultural credit disbursement (takkavi loans) is the matching instrument. The failure mechanism described — official embezzlement, falsified records, negligible output — exactly mirrors the Diwan-i-Kohi's documented failure.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Extension services address knowledge transfer, not financing. The scenario's primary failure mode (fund embezzlement) points to credit disbursement, not technique demonstration.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Grain reserves stabilise food prices but do not restore cultivation capacity — the scenario requires an instrument that finances farmers to cultivate, not one that manages existing grain supply.

Value Addition:
• The takkavi loan concept was revived in colonial India under the Land Improvement Loans Act (1883) and Agriculturists' Loans Act (1884).
• The Diwan-i-Kohi's failure due to corruption anticipates a recurring challenge in state agricultural programmes: the principal-agent problem between government and field officials.
• Post-independence India's Kisan Credit Card and agricultural credit schemes are modern descendants of the same takkavi concept.

solution.concept_anchor: MBT-Ulema conflict — execution of religious figures

statement_analysis.statement: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's interest in philosophy, mathematics, and logic was viewed by the orthodox Ulema as a form of religious heterodoxy incompatible with their conception of correct Islamic governance.
statement_analysis.reason: The orthodox Ulema's hostility to MBT's rationalist and philosophical interests is well-documented — Barani himself frames this as a failing, and the clergy's view that such interests constituted heterodoxy is a historically supported characterisation.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq both marginalised the Ulema from governance for the same reason — their shared conviction that religious scholars had no role in temporal administration.
statement_analysis.reason: While both rulers kept the Ulema at a distance, their motivations differed significantly: Khalji excluded the Ulema primarily to consolidate absolute personal power without religious checks; MBT's distance from the Ulema stemmed from his philosophical rationalism and perceived heterodoxy. The motivations were distinct, not identical.

statement_analysis.statement: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's relationship with Sufi orders was uniformly supportive — he patronised all major Sufi silsilas without exception.
statement_analysis.reason: MBT's relationship with Sufis was complex and not uniformly supportive — he punished some Sufi figures in addition to orthodox clergy, and accounts of tension between him and certain Sufi orders exist. The claim of uniform, unconditional support for all silsilas is an overstatement.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) listing only Statement 2 as incorrect is deceptive because students may correctly identify Statement 2's false equivalence of motivations but miss that Statement 3's 'uniformly supportive' claim is also an overstatement requiring correction.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: orthodox Ulema hostility to MBT's philosophical interests as heterodoxy — historically supported and accurately described; Statement 1 is correct, not incorrect.

Statement 2: 'same reason' for both Khalji and MBT sidelining the Ulema — false equivalence; motivations differed (Khalji = power consolidation; MBT = rationalist temperament); Statement 2 is incorrect.

Statement 3: 'uniformly supportive' of all Sufi silsilas — the word 'uniformly' and 'without exception' make this a false absolute; MBT had tensions with certain Sufi figures; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Two statements (2 and 3) are NOT correct → answer is (c) 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in Statement 2 conflates Khalji's and MBT's motivations for Ulema exclusion by assigning them identical reasoning. Students who know both rulers kept the Ulema at a distance may accept the 'same reason' framing without drilling down into the distinct motivations. Statement 3's trap is a scope-extension — 'uniformly' and 'without exception' are the false qualifiers that turn a partial truth (MBT respected many Sufis) into an overstatement.
solution.final_explanation:
MBT's religious policy operated in a complex triangular space among orthodox Ulema, Sufi orders, and his own rationalist temperament.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Ulema's hostility to MBT's philosophical interests is documented and accurately described. Barani himself frames rationalism and interest in mathematics/logic as deviation from correct Islamic practice.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 'same reason' framing is the error. Alauddin Khalji excluded the Ulema primarily to prevent any institutional check on his absolute authority — a pragmatic power calculation. MBT's distance from the Ulema was rooted in his philosophical rationalism and the clergy's hostility to his heterodox tendencies — a different dynamic entirely.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: MBT's Sufi connections were complex. While he respected prominent Sufis, he also punished certain Sufi figures, and his relationship with different silsilas varied. 'Uniformly supportive without exception' is an overstatement that the historical record does not support.

Value Addition:
• The relationship between Delhi Sultans and the Ulema was a recurring constitutional tension throughout the Sultanate period — Sultans needed Ulema legitimacy but resisted Ulema authority.
• Firuz Tughlaq's reign dramatically reversed this dynamic by actively empowering the Ulema — demonstrating how contested the sultan-clergy relationship was.
• MBT reportedly engaged in theological and philosophical debates — unusual for a medieval sultan and a source of both admiration and suspicion among contemporary observers.

solution.concept_anchor: Rihla authorship and Ibn Battuta's Delhi role
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who know Barani's Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi is a major source may not recall precisely whether Barani also composed a separate work (Fatawa-i-Jahandari is a different work by Barani on political theory), making them accept the false attribution.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): the Futuh-us-Salatin was written by Isami, not by Barani — entity-swap on author; Barani wrote the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi.
Eliminate (c): Ibn Battuta was appointed Qazi (judge) of Delhi, not the Diwan-i-Ariz (military secretary/officer) — entity-swap on the role assigned to Battuta.

Eliminate (d): the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi is Barani's chronicle, but describing it as written 'after Barani fled MBT's court to the Deccan' is incorrect — Barani remained in Delhi, it was Isami who fled to the Deccan; this is an entity-swap of the biographical detail.
Confirm (a): Ibn Battuta authored the Rihla (also called the Tuhfat al-Nuzzar) — this is his travel account; the authorship pair is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) is the most sophisticated trap: it correctly names Barani and the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi but attaches Isami's biographical detail (fleeing to the Deccan) to Barani. Students who know that one chronicler fled to the Deccan but cannot precisely recall which one will be drawn to this option. The entity-swap swaps Isami's geographical/biographical circumstance onto Barani.
solution.final_explanation:
Source attribution is a recurring UPSC competency test for medieval history, and the three major sources for MBT's reign are frequently tested.

• Option (a) — Correct: Ibn Battuta authored the Rihla (full title: Tuhfat al-Nuzzar fi Gharaib al-Amsar wa Ajaib al-Asfar). This is his famous travel account that includes an extended description of his time in Delhi under MBT. The authorship pair is accurately matched.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Futuh-us-Salatin was authored by Isami, not Barani. Barani wrote the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi. This is a straightforward entity-swap between two chroniclers.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Ibn Battuta was appointed Qazi (Islamic judge) of Delhi by MBT — not Diwan-i-Ariz, which was a military administrative role. His judicial appointment is what made him an insider observer.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: While the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi is correctly attributed to Barani, the biographical detail is wrong. It was Isami — not Barani — who composed his work from the Deccan after departing MBT's realm. Barani remained associated with the Delhi court.

Value Addition:
• The full title of Ibn Battuta's work is Tuhfat al-Nuzzar — UPSC sometimes tests this alongside 'Rihla.'
• Barani also wrote the Fatawa-i-Jahandari — a political theory treatise — which is a distinct work from the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi.
• Isami's Futuh-us-Salatin (composed c.1350 in the Bahmani court) is the third major hostile primary source for MBT's reign.

solution.concept_anchor: Implementation capacity vs. policy design — why Khalji succeeded and MBT failed
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students may correctly identify both A and R as true and then assume a causal link exists (MBT failed → therefore Khalji was more practical), without recognising that the revisionist explanation inverts this: it is the state capacity difference, not a difference in the quality of the ideas themselves, that explains the outcome difference.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? The revisionist school (Mohammad Habib) argues that MBT's experiments were conceptually sound but ahead of the medieval state's administrative capacity — this is an accurately described historiographical position. A is correct.
Step 2 — Is R correct? Alauddin Khalji's market reforms and administrative centralisation were successfully implemented and sustained — this is historically accurate. R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? The revisionist thesis about MBT (A) is not explained by Khalji's success (R). The revisionist argument about MBT stands independently on its own logic — it is about the gap between MBT's vision and medieval state capacity. Khalji's success is a separate historical fact that does not causally generate or logically explain the revisionist argument about MBT. If anything, the relationship between them is comparative context, not explanation.
Both A and R are correct, R does NOT explain A → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap makes students think that Khalji's success explains the revisionist thesis about MBT — as if Khalji's achievement proves that MBT's ideas were advanced (because if even Khalji could succeed with simpler tools, MBT's more complex ideas must have been too ambitious). This is faulty causal logic. The revisionist thesis about MBT is self-contained, resting on the gap between vision and state capacity — it does not require Khalji's success as its causal foundation.
solution.final_explanation:
The historiographical comparison between Khalji and MBT is a sophisticated UPSC Mains topic that this question tests at the Prelims level.

Assertion (A): Correct. The revisionist school — led by Mohammad Habib — argues precisely this: MBT's token currency, Daulatabad transfer, Diwan-i-Kohi, and Khorasan plan were conceptually rational but presupposed a state apparatus with enforcement capacity, audit mechanisms, and public trust that the medieval Sultanate did not possess. The ideas were ahead of their time; the institutions were not.

Reason (R): Correct. Khalji's reforms — price controls, market inspectors, grain reserves, standardised measurement — were implemented successfully. This is historically undisputed.

Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The revisionist thesis about MBT is internally generated — it is about the mismatch between MBT's ambitions and medieval administrative capacity. Khalji's success is a separately relevant comparative fact but does not causally produce or logically explain the revisionist argument. The relationship between the two facts is contextual comparison, not causation.

Value Addition:
• The revisionist school explicitly rehabilitates MBT by arguing that 'bad implementation' rather than 'bad ideas' was the cause of failure — a significant interpretive shift from Lane-Poole's 'eccentric tyrant' narrative.
• The Marxist interpretation adds a structural layer: feudal sultanate structures were incompatible with MBT's quasi-rational reforms regardless of personal capacity.
• For UPSC Mains: a good answer on MBT explicitly acknowledges the revisionist-traditional debate rather than adopting either position uncritically.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who know both the Shahna-i-Mandi and takkavi loans are state economic interventions may conflate them — the Shahna-i-Mandi supervised markets (a Khalji instrument) but students may pair it with MBT's agricultural credit instead.

Match B (Token copper/brass currency): MBT's representative currency experiment — matches with 1 (attempt to substitute base-metal tokens for silver tankas).

The Shahna-i-Mandi (Khalji) and the Diwan-i-Kohi (MBT) are both economic interventions but belong to entirely different reform systems — students who do not maintain sharp ruler-instrument associations will cross-match them.

Correct Matches:

• B (Token copper/brass currency) → 1: MBT's monetary experiment — declaring base-metal tokens equivalent to silver tankas — was an attempt to address the silver shortage through representative currency.
• C (Diwan-i-Kohi) → 4: MBT's dedicated agriculture ministry, tasked with bringing barren land under cultivation and demonstrating improved farming — a unique institutional creation.
• D (Public grain reserves) → 2: Khalji's strategic grain storage system, used to stabilise food prices by releasing stored grain during shortages — a supply-management instrument.

statement_analysis.statement: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's scholarly interests included logic, philosophy, mathematics, and medicine — a range that made him intellectually distinctive among the rulers of the Delhi Sultanate.
statement_analysis.reason: MBT's proficiency in logic, philosophy, mathematics, and medicine is documented by multiple sources including Battuta's admiring accounts — this breadth of scholarly interest was indeed unusual among Delhi Sultans.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Ziauddin Barani and Ibn Battuta provide entirely negative assessments of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's character, describing him as cruel, impractical, and religiously deviant without any positive qualities.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a scope-extension error. Barani is predominantly critical but acknowledges MBT's learning and generosity as well as condemning his cruelty — his characterisation as 'a mixture of opposites' is ambivalent, not purely negative. Battuta is explicitly ambivalent — admiring MBT's extraordinary generosity while recording his cruelty.

statement_analysis.statement: The historiographical debate over Muhammad bin Tughlaq — whether he was a visionary ruler undone by circumstances or a dangerously impractical one — reflects a genuine interpretive divide rather than a settled scholarly consensus.
statement_analysis.reason: The revisionist school (Habib) and the traditional school (Lane-Poole and others influenced by medieval hostile sources) represent two genuinely distinct and maintained historiographical positions — no consensus has emerged, making the debate a live interpretive question.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three correct' is the strongest distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are correct and broadly known, tempting students to accept Statement 2 without scrutinising whether both Barani and Battuta were actually uniformly negative.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: MBT's scholarly interests in logic, philosophy, mathematics, and medicine — documented across multiple sources including Battuta; Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: 'entirely negative assessments' without 'any positive qualities' — this is a scope-extension; both Barani and Battuta record positive qualities (generosity, learning) alongside criticism; the 'entirely negative' claim is factually wrong; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: the revisionist-traditional historiographical divide is genuine and unresolved — accurately described; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (b) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 adds 'entirely negative' and 'without any positive qualities' to convert a partial truth (both authors are critical) into a false absolute. Students who know Barani was harsh and Battuta was ambivalent may still accept 'entirely negative' if they haven't precisely fixed the distinction between Barani's mixed verdict and Battuta's explicit admiration for MBT's generosity. The trap rewards students who recall that Battuta's Rihla contains genuine praise for MBT's extraordinary gifts.
solution.final_explanation:
MBT's character assessment by primary sources and the subsequent historiographical debate are both UPSC-relevant themes.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The scholarly range attributed to MBT — logic, philosophy, mathematics, medicine — is consistently reported and represents a genuine distinction within the Delhi Sultanate's roster of rulers. This breadth contributed both to his reformist vision and to orthodox clergy hostility.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This statement universalises both sources into 'entirely negative' — a false reading of both. Barani's 'mixture of opposites' formulation explicitly acknowledges MBT's generosity and learning before condemning his cruelty and rationalism. Battuta's Rihla is explicitly ambivalent — containing some of the most admiring descriptions of MBT's generosity in medieval literature alongside accounts of his brutal punishments.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The revisionist (Habib) versus traditional (Lane-Poole) divide is genuinely unresolved. Different historiographical schools maintain different positions based on different weightings of primary evidence and structural versus personal explanations of failure.

Value Addition:
• MBT reportedly wrote poetry in Persian — adding a literary dimension to his scholarly profile.
• Battuta records that MBT could conduct sophisticated theological and philosophical debates — an unusual skill for a medieval ruler.
• The absence of any fully sympathetic contemporary source means MBT's positive qualities are documented primarily by those who also condemned him — making source-critical reading essential.

The founding of the Bahmani Sultanate occurred in 1347 — approximately eleven years after Vijayanagara.
Correct sequence: Daulatabad transfer (1327) → Vijayanagara founding (1336) → Bahmani founding (1347) → matches option (c): 1 → 3 → 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits students' tendency to learn Vijayanagara and Bahmani as a paired fact ('both founded during MBT's reign') without fixing their relative order. 1336 (Vijayanagara) before 1347 (Bahmani) is the correct sequence — the eleven-year gap is often collapsed in memory. Option (b) reverses this, which is the most attractive wrong answer for a student who knows both dates approximately but not precisely.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of the most consequential events of MBT's reign can be sequenced precisely using the dates 1327, 1336, and 1347.

Correct sequence: 1 → 3 → 2

1. Transfer of capital to Daulatabad (~1327): The earliest major experiment, initiated in the second year of MBT's reign. Its reversal and the administrative chaos it caused set the stage for subsequent rebellions.

3. Founding of Vijayanagara (1336): Harihara I and Bukka Raya I established the kingdom in 1336 — approximately nine years after the capital transfer, during the period of maximum administrative disruption in the Deccan.

2. Founding of Bahmani Sultanate (1347): Hasan Gangu's rebellion and the establishment of the Bahmani Sultanate came twenty years into MBT's reign — a direct product of the accumulated failure of his Deccan administration.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a) 2 → 3 → 1: Places Bahmani before Vijayanagara and before the Daulatabad transfer — both reversals are incorrect.
• Option (b) 1 → 2 → 3: Places Bahmani (1347) before Vijayanagara (1336) — the most common temporal reversal.
• Option (d) 3 → 1 → 2: Places Vijayanagara before the Daulatabad transfer — impossible; the transfer occurred in 1327, Vijayanagara in 1336.

Value Addition:
• All three events are causally linked: the Daulatabad transfer disrupted Deccan administration → creating the vacuum in which first Vijayanagara, then Bahmani emerged.
• By 1347 (Bahmani founding), MBT had effectively lost the Deccan permanently — four years before his death in 1351.
• The eleven-year gap between Vijayanagara (1336) and Bahmani (1347) reflects different stages of Deccan fragmentation.

solution.concept_anchor: Khorasan army size — 3,70,000 soldiers maintained for one year
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because 3,00,000 is a plausible round number close to the reported figure, and students who recall 'approximately three lakh soldiers' may select it without knowing the specifically recorded figure of 3,70,000.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): 1,00,000 is too low — this figure does not match any recorded account of the Khorasan army and would not constitute an 'enormous' drain on the treasury in context.
Eliminate (c): 3,00,000 is close but not the specifically recorded figure — the distinction between 3 lakh and 3.7 lakh is the precision UPSC tests.
Eliminate (d): 5,00,000 is larger than the recorded figure and not consistent with historical accounts.
Confirm (b): 3,70,000 is the specific figure recorded by historical accounts for the Khorasan expedition army — both the number and the one-year maintenance period are testable facts.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap here operates on numerical proximity — students who remember 'approximately three lakh' will be drawn to option (c) rather than recognising the specifically recorded 3,70,000. The distinction requires precise number recall rather than approximate order-of-magnitude knowledge, which is exactly how UPSC tests quantitative historical data.
solution.final_explanation:
The Khorasan expedition plan represents one of history's most expensive military non-events — a treasury-draining exercise that produced no military engagement.

• Option (a) 1,00,000 — Incorrect: One lakh is too small to qualify as the fiscally ruinous force that historical accounts describe; not the recorded figure.
• Option (b) 3,70,000 — Correct: Historical accounts record the Khorasan army at approximately 3,70,000 soldiers, maintained at enormous cost for roughly one year before being disbanded without any military deployment.
• Option (c) 3,00,000 — Incorrect: Three lakh is close but not the specific figure recorded — precision is required here.
• Option (d) 5,00,000 — Incorrect: Five lakh exceeds the recorded figure and is not consistent with historical accounts of the expedition.

Value Addition:
• The Khorasan army cost is often cited as one of the single largest treasury drains in Sultanate history — equivalent to a year of war expenditure with no military return.
• The decision to raise such an army and then disband it without deployment reflects MBT's tendency toward grand planning with inadequate follow-through on geopolitical realities.
• Contemporary critics like Barani specifically condemned the Khorasan plan as an example of MBT's reckless fiscal management — spending without strategic return.

solution.concept_anchor: MBT sultanate as 'cradle of successor states'
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know the Deccan Sultanates emerged later may conflate the five Deccan Sultanates (which emerged from the Bahmani Sultanate's fragmentation in the early 16th century) with the direct breakaway kingdoms of MBT's period.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): the five Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar) emerged from the fragmentation of the Bahmani Sultanate in the 15th–16th centuries, not directly during MBT's reign.
Eliminate (b): the Mughal Empire was founded by Babur in 1526 — nearly 175 years after MBT's death in 1351; no causal 'cradle' relationship applies here.

Confirm (c): Vijayanagara (1336) and Bahmani (1347) both emerged during MBT's reign as direct products of his Deccan policy failures — these are the two successor states most directly and causally connected to MBT's collapse of authority.

Eliminate (d): the Bengal Sultanate had been gradually drifting toward independence since earlier in the 14th century and does not pair naturally with Vijayanagara as 'the two kingdoms' most directly enabled by MBT's Deccan failures specifically.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in option (a) plants the five Deccan Sultanates — a well-known medieval fact — as if they were MBT-era creations. Students who know that Deccan fragmentation is associated with the Bahmani Sultanate's history may accept this without checking the timeline (the five Deccan Sultanates emerged a century and a half after MBT). Option (d) adds Bengal as a plausible second kingdom alongside Vijayanagara, exploiting the knowledge that Bengal did rebel — but Bengal did not produce a kingdom with the same direct causal connection to Deccan policy failures.
solution.final_explanation:
The characterisation of MBT's sultanate as a 'cradle of successor states' refers specifically to the two permanent southern kingdoms that emerged directly from his failures.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The five Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar) emerged from the fragmentation of the Bahmani Sultanate between 1490 and 1530 — approximately 140–180 years after MBT's death. They are not 'direct emergences' from MBT's reign.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Mughal Empire (est. 1526 by Babur) has no causal connection to MBT's policy failures — it emerged from an entirely different historical process involving Timurid and Central Asian dynamics.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Vijayanagara kingdom (1336) and the Bahmani Sultanate (1347) are the two kingdoms that directly and causally emerged from MBT's failure to maintain Deccan authority — both founded during his reign, both by figures connected to his administration.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: While Bengal did assert independence during and after MBT's reign, it does not pair with Vijayanagara in the 'Deccan policy failure' context. Bengal's drift toward independence had earlier roots and a different dynamic.

Value Addition:
• Vijayanagara and Bahmani were rival kingdoms for two centuries — their mutual antagonism shaped Deccan politics until Vijayanagara's defeat at the Battle of Talikota (1565).
• Both kingdoms' founders had personal connections to the Delhi Sultanate — Harihara/Bukka as officers, Hasan Gangu as a rebel governor.
• The permanent loss of the Deccan under MBT meant that no subsequent Delhi Sultan ever regained meaningful control over South India.

solution.concept_anchor: Diwan-i-Kohi vs. Firuz canal irrigation — implementation modality contrast

statement_analysis.statement: The Diwan-i-Kohi under Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firuz Tughlaq's canal irrigation projects both represented state investment in agriculture, but they adopted different implementation modalities — the former relied on administrative machinery and direct state farming, while the latter focused on physical infrastructure investment.
statement_analysis.reason: The Diwan-i-Kohi used an administrative-institutional approach (creating a ministry, state farms, disbursing loans through officials), while Firuz Tughlaq's success came through canal construction — physical infrastructure that worked independently of official integrity once built. This implementation modality difference is historically supported.

statement_analysis.statement: Firuz Tughlaq's agricultural policies succeeded for the same reasons that Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Diwan-i-Kohi failed — because Firuz employed honest officials while MBT employed corrupt ones.
statement_analysis.reason: The success-failure contrast is not primarily explained by official honesty vs. corruption but by implementation modality: Firuz invested in physical infrastructure (canals) that functioned independently of ongoing official conduct, whereas MBT's approach depended entirely on official integrity for disbursement and record-keeping — a structural difference, not merely a personnel difference.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) 'both correct' is the actual correct answer here but students may doubt Statement 1's nuanced modality distinction, making them retreat to option (c) thinking Statement 1 is an overinterpretation.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: the Diwan-i-Kohi used administrative/institutional means (ministry, state farms, official-mediated loans) while Firuz used infrastructure (canals) — this modality distinction is historically accurate and analytically supported; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: attributing the success-failure contrast solely to official honesty vs. corruption is an oversimplification that misses the structural infrastructure vs. administration distinction; this reduces a structural explanation to a personnel explanation; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The contrast between MBT's Diwan-i-Kohi and Firuz Tughlaq's canal system is a standard UPSC analytical comparison that tests depth of institutional understanding.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The key difference is implementation modality. MBT's approach was administrative — create a ministry, appoint officials, give them funds and authority. This approach collapsed when officials embezzled funds and falsified records. Firuz Tughlaq's canal construction created physical infrastructure that, once built, functioned independently of ongoing official behaviour. Water flows through a canal regardless of whether the official who built it was honest — the infrastructure was self-sustaining in a way that administrative structures are not.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This reduces a structural difference to a personnel difference. Both administrations likely had some honest and some corrupt officials. The real distinction is that physical infrastructure (canals) does not require continuous official integrity to deliver its benefits, whereas administrative disbursement schemes (takkavi loans, Diwan-i-Kohi grants) are entirely dependent on ongoing official honesty. Statement 2 misidentifies the cause of the contrast.

Value Addition:
• Firuz Tughlaq built several major canals connecting rivers to agricultural areas — among the earliest large-scale irrigation infrastructure projects in medieval India.
• The principal-agent problem (gap between the authority's intent and the implementing official's incentives) is the structural explanation for why MBT's Diwan-i-Kohi failed.
• This contrast is a classic 'institutions vs. infrastructure' development economics question applied to medieval Indian history.

solution.concept_anchor: Barani's ideological bias — what he omits matters as much as what he records

statement_analysis.statement: Ziauddin Barani's Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi is the most comprehensive contemporary account of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign, and its orthodox Sunni ideological framework means that what Barani chooses to omit is as historiographically significant as what he records.
statement_analysis.reason: Barani's text is indeed a primary chronicle of MBT's reign, and scholars widely acknowledge that his ideological framework (orthodox Sunni, aristocratic) shaped what he included and excluded — the significance of his omissions is a standard historiographical observation.

statement_analysis.statement: Ibn Battuta's reliability as a source for MBT's reign is unimpeachable because he served as Qazi of Delhi and therefore had official access to state records and judicial proceedings.
statement_analysis.reason: Official access does not make a source unimpeachable: Battuta composed the Rihla from memory years after leaving Delhi, introducing the risk of error and exaggeration; some of his accounts are considered embellished or borrowed. His inside position improves but does not guarantee his reliability.

statement_analysis.statement: The numismatic evidence from Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency period constitutes an independent archaeological source that can partially corroborate or complicate the narrative provided by literary sources like Barani and Battuta.
statement_analysis.reason: Token currency coins from MBT's period are material evidence that archaeology and numismatics use to corroborate, nuance, or challenge textual accounts — the characterisation of this as an independent source that can 'corroborate or complicate' literary accounts is methodologically accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) listing Statement 2 only as incorrect is the natural trap for students who identify Battuta's reliability problem but miss that Statements 1 and 3 are both correct — tempting them to choose (b) when the correct answer is (d) which also lists only Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Barani's text as comprehensive chronicle + ideological omissions as historiographically significant — both accurate; Statement 1 is correct, not incorrect.

Statement 2: 'unimpeachable' reliability — false absolute; inside access does not guarantee reliability; retrospective composition from memory and possible exaggeration are documented reliability concerns; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: numismatic evidence as independent source that can 'corroborate or complicate' literary accounts — methodologically accurate; Statement 3 is correct, not incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct → answer is (d) 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 2 takes a true fact (Battuta was Qazi with official access) and draws an unwarranted absolute conclusion ('unimpeachable reliability'). Students who know Battuta was an insider observer may accept the reliability claim without applying the additional knowledge that the Rihla was composed retrospectively from memory — a documented reliability limitation. 'Unimpeachable' is the false qualifier converting a partial truth into an incorrect claim.
solution.final_explanation:
Evaluating the strengths and limitations of primary sources is a core UPSC historiographical skill.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Barani's Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi is the major chronicle and its ideological shaping of both inclusions and exclusions is a recognised historiographical point. What Barani chooses not to record — MBT's administrative innovations he disapproved of, or positive reception of heterodox ideas — is as telling as his criticisms.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This is the trap. Official access improves but cannot guarantee reliability. Battuta's Rihla was composed from memory years after he left Delhi — a process introducing error, exaggeration, and potentially borrowed accounts. Some of his more dramatic descriptions are treated with scholarly scepticism. 'Unimpeachable' is a false absolute.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Surviving token currency coins from MBT's period are material evidence studied by numismatists. They can confirm the existence of the experiment, provide details of design and inscription, and either align with or complicate textual accounts — making them a genuinely independent evidentiary layer.

Value Addition:
• The methodology of using multiple source types (literary, epigraphic, numismatic, archaeological) to cross-check medieval history is called multi-source corroboration — increasingly important in UPSC Mains source-evaluation questions.
• Battuta's text went through an editorial process involving Ibn Juzayy, who helped write it — another layer of potential modification between observation and final text.
• Barani's selective silence on MBT's promotion of Hindu officials is itself a form of evidence — his aristocratic ideology made this too uncomfortable to elaborate.
